item.title: Classic Rock Fridays! Music Appreciation-The Best Rock of the 60s, 70s, and 80s — Fri Nov 27, 9:30 PM
item.description:
Try New Things in Toronto! Good day everyone,
Join us this Friday night at The Pheasant for a laid-back and at time upbeat evening of classic rock! Grab a pint, catch up with old friends or meet some new ones, and enjoy great rock from the ’60s, ’70s, and ’80s. If a favourite song gets you out of your chair, feel free to get up and dance! ㅤ
* **The ’60s** brought us the Beatles, the Rolling Stones, C.C.R., The Kinks, The Animlas, The Who, The Jimy Hendrix Experience, The Beach Boys and the Doors, from the British Invasion to psychedelic rock. * **The ’70s** gave us Led Zeppelin, Fleetwood Mac, The Eagles, Aerosmith, Heart, Queen, Boston, Pink Floyd, David Bowie and Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers, with big guitar riffs and songs you still know by heart. * **The ’80s** brought us Bruce Springsteen, John Mellencamp, ZZ Top, AC DC, Journey, Billy Idol, Van Halen Def Leppard, Joan Jett, Pat Benatar, Guns n' Roses The Police and Bon Jovi, with arena anthems and plenty to sing along to.
ㅤ

item.title: Civic Meetup #571: The New Civic Architects: Rise of the Entrepreneurial Social Club — Tue Dec 1, 7:00 PM — Online: https://link.civictech.ca/zoom
item.description:
Topic: The New Civic Architects: Rise of the Entrepreneurial Social Club
In an increasingly isolated, digital, and fragmented economy, people have gotten very entrepreneurial about community building. House parties, "going to the bar", and other unstructured activities have fallen by the wayside in favour of highly structured, curated, sometimes-professionally-useful, often ticketed, community event series -- especially for Gen Z.
While critics worry about the commercialization of friendship, this talk explores what is actually driving this boom, and explores why a small army of entrepreneurial community builders might just be the civic architects we need to absorb the economic shockwaves of the next decade.
‎
Speaker: Joss Murphy (in-person)
Joss is the cofounder and CEO of Wygo, where she builds tools for entrepreneurial community event organizers to scale their businesses and organizations sustainably.

item.title: I Can Do What I Want Now — Tue Dec 1, 7:00 PM — Online
item.description:
Queer Death Salon is a virtual community space for all 2SLGBTQIA+ people to come together to discuss death, dying and grief. In this Queer Death Salon, Carta Monir roots us in her own experience of coming out as trans around the time that her mom was diagnosed with terminal cancer, and the way her mother's death allowed her to express her womanhood in ways that she previously thought were impossible.. Participants will explore the authenticity and permission for queer expression that can be created at the end of a loved one's life, and after. 18+ imagery and themes will be integrated in this salon. Carta Monir is a writer, visual artist, and sex worker living in Michigan. She was an artist in residence at the Tom of Finland Foundation, and her work has been exhibited and screened internationally. Her work deals with pain, disability, trauma, and perseverance. https://cartamonir.com/ Photo credit: Cody Sells ‍
Source: YOHOMO

Bring your family and find your inner rhythm by joining us on stage in the Nanji Family Foundation Auditorium for a special drumming workshop.
Join artist Amadou Kienou for a hands-on drumming workshop introducing participants to West African culture and traditions. Learn different drumming techniques and rhythms on the djembé while connecting with others.
The djembé is more than a musical instrument, it is a form of communication used to send messages from village to village, city to city, and country to country. Learn about its role in West African culture and how it brings people together through music.

item.description: Queer Death Salon is a virtual community space for all 2SLGBTQIA+ people to come together to discuss death, dying and grief. Badly Licked Bear will lead participants in a discussion on scars, wounds, illness, and disability. Like trees in a rainforest, our bodies are simultaneously places of growth and decay; parallel forces that define and carry us and guide us towards the final disposition. We'll explore what it feels like to experience our progress towards death, in particular the permanent changes to our bodies, minds, and spirits that come as out physical bodies continue to grow and change. Let's gather and share reflections on the ways we live our lives; fully, and in part, as people who often feel like part of ourselves, or that part of ourselves that we once knew is now gone, or with the reminders of the experiences that have left their marks on us.
